rationale: The pooled forest probably wastes splits learning study differences (sequencing depth, 16S region, protocol) instead of disease signal, and scoring is within each study anyway. I'll replace each genus's relative abundance with its percentile rank within its own study. This keeps the within-study ordering that the metric cares about and removes the between-study shifts. It uses no labels and uses study only for harmonization.

IBD dysbiosis is consistently linked to lower alpha diversity, and a random forest splitting on single genus ranks can only pick that up indirectly. I'll add explicit diversity features (OTU and genus Shannon, inverse Simpson, and expected richness rarefied analytically to a common depth within each study), each converted to a percentile rank within its study, so the forest has a direct signal that sequencing depth doesn't distort.

Right now every OTU with no genus assignment (`g__`) is summed into one column, whatever its family. Unclassified Lachnospiraceae, Ruminococcaceae and Enterobacteriaceae are large parts of the gut community and move in opposite directions in IBD. I'll group OTUs by their lineage down to genus, so unclassified OTUs keep their family/order identity and same-named genera in different families stay apart. Since IBD signals are often clearest at family level, this should give the forest cleaner features; the per-study rank harmonization stays as it is.

Pooled over four studies there are probably hundreds of genera, and most are rare or are 16S-region artefacts. Their percentile ranks are almost all tied zeros, so they mainly carry study-specific noise, and they crowd out the informative genera from each split's random `sqrt` feature subset. I'll keep only genera present (count > 0) in at least 10% of samples in at least one study. This filter uses no labels and keeps genera that are common only in some studies. Everything else is unchanged: the per-study rank harmonization and the random forest.

The fraction of cases differs a lot between studies, so the pooled forest gains by learning which study a sample came from. It can do that easily, for example from genera that are absent in a whole study and so all get the same rank of about 0.5. That signal is useless for within-study AUROC. I'll weight each training sample by 1/(number of samples in its study × class cell), so every study is class-balanced and study identity stops predicting disease. The forest should then spend its splits on disease signal that holds within each study.

IBD dysbiosis is mostly a broad, additive shift: many Clostridiales genera such as Faecalibacterium and Roseburia go down together while Enterobacteriaceae and others go up. A random forest that splits on one genus at a time picks up that kind of signal noisily. I'll average the rank-transformed predictions of the current forest with a study/class-balanced L2 logistic regression on the same per-study genus ranks. The regression's strength is tuned by grouped inner CV on the training fold, and the two models should make errors that partly cancel.

Many IBD shifts happen across whole families: Enterobacteriaceae and Fusobacteriaceae go up, Ruminococcaceae and Lachnospiraceae go down. At genus level, a large share of these reads sits in the single merged `g__` column, so the signal is split up or blurred. I'll add family-level relative abundances, ranked within each study like the genus features. Round 3 replaced the genus features and lost score; this time the genus features stay as they are and the family features are added alongside, giving both models cleaner aggregate signals.

The logistic regression currently uses the same within-study percentile ranks as the forest. Ranks throw away fold-change size and ignore that the data are compositional. IBD dysbiosis is a broad shift in log-ratios (Clostridiales down, Proteobacteria up), so I'll give the regression its own features: genus-level CLR values, computed from counts with a 0.5 pseudocount and z-scored within each study. The forest keeps the rank features it does well with. This should make the regression stronger and less correlated with the forest.

Right now a zero count gets a different feature value depending on the study. If a genus is never detected in a study, its tied average rank is about 0.5, which reads as "middling abundance". If it is detected in some samples, its zeros rank low. I'll map every zero to 0 and keep each nonzero value's within-study percentile rank, so "not detected" means the same thing in every study and the absent-genus study fingerprint goes away. Ordering within each study is unchanged, so this should give both models cleaner, more transferable splits and coefficients.

rationale: This retries round 9's idea with the crash fixed. Round 9 tried to write into a read-only array. Now the per-study ranks are copied into a writable array with `np.array(..., copy=True)` before zeros are overwritten. Every zero count is set to 0, and nonzero values keep their within-study percentile rank. "Not detected" then means the same in every study, and a genus missing from a whole study no longer gets a tied rank of about 0.5, which had been acting as a study fingerprint.

I'm adding one label-free, literature-defined feature: the Gevers 2014 microbial dysbiosis index. It is the log ratio of IBD-enriched families (Enterobacteriaceae, Pasteurellaceae, Veillonellaceae, Fusobacteriaceae) to IBD-depleted orders (Bacteroidales, Clostridiales, Erysipelotrichales), computed from the full lineages and ranked within each study. It pools the shift that is currently scattered across many noisy genus columns, including reads in the merged `g__` column, into one dense, harmonized signal that both the forest and the regression can use.

The forest uses fully grown trees with large balanced sample weights on small study×class cells, so its leaves tend to memorize a few heavily weighted samples. I'll add an ExtraTrees model with the same balanced weights and `min_samples_leaf=3`. Its random split thresholds give smoother, lower-variance votes on the tied-zero rank features, and it splits the tree half of the rank average with the current forest while the logistic regression keeps its half.

I'm adding a shallow, strongly regularized LightGBM as a third member of the equal-weight rank average. It uses the same per-study genus ranks and the same study/class-balanced weights as the other two models. IBD dysbiosis involves conditional, threshold-like interactions, for example Enterobacteriaceae blooms mattering mainly when butyrate producers are depleted. Boosting fits those residual patterns sequentially, which neither the bagged forest nor the additive logistic regression does, so its errors should partly cancel theirs.

Each model's predictions are currently ranked across the pooled test set before averaging. If one model's scores for a given study fall in a narrow band because of study-level offsets, that model has little say inside that study, which is what the metric scores. I'll rank each model's predictions within each test study before averaging, so all three models get equal weight inside every study. This uses study only to harmonize outputs, not as a predictor.

Sequencing depth varies roughly tenfold even within a single study. A low-abundance genus therefore reads as "detected" in deep samples and as zero in shallow ones, so the zero-mapped ranks partly measure depth, not biology. I'll give each study a common detection limit: any genus whose relative abundance is below 1 / (that study's 10th-percentile depth) is set to zero before the within-study ranking. This makes presence/absence comparable across samples without the random noise of real rarefaction, and the ordering of abundant genera is unchanged.

IBD dysbiosis hits whole guilds of bacteria together, such as the butyrate-producing Clostridiales and the oral or facultative bloomers, but each genus on its own is sparse and noisy. I'll add about 20 co-abundance-group features. To build them, I cluster the prevalent genera using the average of their within-study Spearman correlations. Each sample then gets the mean genus rank within each group, re-ranked within its study, alongside the existing genus ranks. The groups come from the abundance data only (no labels) and are built the same way in every study, so all three models get dense, low-noise guild signals.

I'm adding the dysbiosis score from Lloyd-Price 2019 / Halfvarson 2017, a known IBD signal. For each sample it is the median Bray-Curtis distance to the training controls from the same study, plus the same distance to the training cases and the difference between the two. Distances are computed on genus relative abundance, excluding the sample's own subject so it can't match its repeat visits. Each feature is then mapped through its study's training distribution so every study is on the same scale. All three models get this whole-community "how far from healthy" signal, which a single genus feature can't express.

Some subjects contribute several longitudinal stool samples, so the current per-(study, class) weights let a few heavily sampled subjects dominate each cell. All three models can then memorize those individuals' microbiomes instead of learning disease signal that generalizes across subjects (CV is grouped by subject). I'll down-weight each sample by 1/(number of that subject's samples in training) before the study×class balancing, so each subject counts once in its cell. This applies to the forest, the boosting model, and the logistic regression's inner CV. If every subject has only one sample, nothing changes.

The metric is the unweighted mean of per-study AUROCs. The current weights still give each study training mass in proportion to its size, so the largest cohort (Gevers RISK) dominates every model. I'll make each study's total mass proportional to the square root of its size instead. This is still class-balanced within each study, and it gives the smaller studies (which count equally in the score) more say without putting all the weight on a few samples. It applies to the forest, the logistic regression and its inner CV, and LightGBM.

I'll cut the existing label-free co-abundance dendrogram at a second, coarser level (6 groups) alongside the current 20. The aim is a few dense features for the broad IBD guilds, such as butyrate-producing Clostridiales versus facultative or oral bloomers. At 20 groups those guilds are split into small, noisy pieces. The genus ranks, the 20-group CAGs, the weights and the 3-model ensemble stay unchanged.
